stem: A nurse is preparing to access an implanted venous port for chemotherapy in an outpatient oncology clinic. Which action is appropriate?

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, inspect and cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, and access the septum with a non-coring needle.
options.B: Use a standard hypodermic needle because any sterile needle can safely penetrate the port septum.
options.C: Omit skin antisepsis when the port has been accessed recently and the skin appears clean.
options.D: Access the port before inspecting the surrounding chest and neck so manipulation does not alter the assessment findings.

rationale: CDC outpatient oncology guidance for implanted ports directs the nurse to perform hand hygiene, examine the site and surrounding chest/neck for complications, cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, stabilize the portal body, and insert a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle until the portal backing is felt. CDC notes that clean or sterile gloves may be used for implanted-port access and that professional-society recommendations differ, so the final item does not incorrectly require one universal glove type. A standard hypodermic needle, skipped antisepsis, or access before site assessment is not consistent with the described procedure.
educational_objective: Apply evidence-based implanted-port access steps, including pre-access assessment, skin antisepsis, and use of a non-coring needle without overstating a universal sterile-glove requirement.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Basic Infection Control and Prevention Plan for Outpatient Oncology Settings
source_locator: Section VI, Central venous catheters; Section VI.D.1, Implanted Ports — Port Access Procedure
source_claim_supported: CDC's implanted-port access procedure includes hand hygiene, examination of the site and veins of the chest and neck, clean or sterile gloves, cleansing with an appropriate antiseptic, stabilization of the portal body, and insertion of a non-coring needle such as a Huber needle.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic technique, invasive-device care, and infection-prevention nursing activities
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe access of an implanted central venous port
correction_summary: Rebuilt the original port-access item to remove the unsupported universal phrase 'strict sterile technique' and the implication that sterile gloves are always required. Replaced the generic ONS homepage with CDC's exact implanted-port procedure. Preserved the clinically important requirements for pre-access assessment, antisepsis, and a non-coring needle while making all distractors concrete procedural errors.
audit_findings: Original wording overstated 'strict sterile technique' as a universal port-access requirement despite CDC noting no consensus over clean versus sterile gloves for implanted ports.
CDC directly supports pre-access inspection, hand hygiene, appropriate skin antisepsis, and use of a non-coring needle for implanted-port access.
The final item avoids duplicating Q1744's tunneled-catheter connector-disinfection construct by focusing specifically on implanted-port access equipment and site preparation.
All distractors conflict with explicit procedural elements and no second defensible answer remains.
Independent adversarial review found no ambiguity, cueing, unsupported glove requirement, or unresolved source conflict.
